chunks: The discussion of it is that we say: As for the first segment of his statement, 'We prove to the Imamiyah that occultation involves an evil aspect,' it is a mere promise from him not accompanied by an argument. He should have clarified the 'evil aspect' which he wanted to prove to them, so we could consider it, but he did not, so his promise is not directed.

And if he said that as a questioner in a certain manner: 'What do you reject about there being an evil aspect in it?' Then we say: The evil aspects are conceivable in the context of the thing being oppression, vanity, lie, debauchery, and ignorance, and none of these are present here, so we know by that the non-existence of the evil aspect.

If it is said: The evil aspect is that the cause of the obligated one was not removed according to your view, because his outstretched hand, which is kindness in reality, and the fear of his discipline did not occur, so that became a lack of kindness to the obligated one, thus it is evil because of it.

key_terms.عِلَّةَ الْمُكَلَّف: The cause/reason for the obligated one

ai.seo_question: How does Al-Tusi refute the claim that the occultation of the Imam involves an evil aspect?
ai.summary: Al-Tusi employs the Usuli principle of 'qubh aqli' (rational evil) to refute the claim that the Imam's occultation is inherently flawed, arguing that the opponent failed to specify a concrete defect such as injustice or ignorance. He specifically counters the argument that the withholding of the Imam's physical authority (yad al-intisar) negates the divine kindness (lutf), asserting that the occultation itself is a distinct form of benevolent protection rather than a failure of duty. This defense solidifies the theological legitimacy of the Hidden Imam's status during the Major Occultation.

en.sayyid-athar-husain-s-h-rizvi: Reply: The first segment of his argument that, “We prove to the Imamiyah that occultation involves an evil aspect,” is a mere promise that he makes. He should have explained “the evil aspect”, which he wanted to prove to the Imamiyah, so it would have been possible for us to consider it and reply to it. He has not done that and therefore his argument is inconclusive.

If he asks, “Do you reject that occultation involves a wrong aspect?” Our response would be that wrong aspects are conceivable in the context of oppression, vanity, lie, debauchery and ignorance, and none of these are involved here. This leads us to reject the instance of any wrong aspect.
